summary: By the end, learners can name the main Google Workspace apps, open Google Drive, create a Google Doc and a Google Sheet, and share a file with Viewer, Commenter, or Editor access — without treating this course as a Google credential.

lessons.title: What is Google Workspace?
lessons.html:
Google Workspace is a set of apps you can use in a web browser. Google’s Workspace Learning Center says you can start with apps such as Gmail, Docs, and Drive, and work from different devices.

The same Learning Center groups the apps by what they help you do:

  • Connect: Gmail (email), Calendar, Chat, and Meet (video and voice meetings)
  • Create: Docs (word processing), Sheets (spreadsheets), Slides (presentations), and Forms (surveys and quizzes)
  • Store and find files: Drive (cloud storage)

You do not need every app for this course. The next lessons practise Drive, Docs, Sheets, and sharing. A later Range Path course covers Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint if those are the tools at your site. This course does not replace those Microsoft courses, and it is not a full Gmail or Meet class.

If your council, library, or workplace gives you a work or school Google account, your administrator may turn some features on or off. If you use your own account, follow the sign-in they approve on that computer. This course will not create an account for you and will not ask you to type a password into the lesson.

Google’s help also notes accessibility options in the Learning Center. Ask your instructor if you need those tools.

lessons.title: Find your files in Google Drive
lessons.html:
Google Drive helps you keep files together. Google’s Drive help says you can upload and share files, create new files, keep them organized, and open them from different devices.

On a computer:

  1. Go to drive.google.com.
  2. At the top left, click New.
  3. Choose what you need: New folder, Folder upload, a document type (to create a file), or File upload.

My Drive holds files and folders you upload or sync, and Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Forms you create. Files that other people shared with you appear in Shared with me.

The Home section can show files you or others recently opened, shared, or edited. You can search and use filters such as type, people, modified date, or location.

To see information about a file, click it and choose View details. That can include activity, sharing permissions, and recent changes.

To move a file you no longer need out of the way, Google says you can select it and choose Move to trash.

Do not upload someone else’s private documents for practise. Use a sample file you created, or a practise file your instructor gives you.

If you use a work or school account, your organization may set extra rules. Follow those rules.

lessons.title: Create a Google Doc
lessons.html:
Google Docs is the word-processing app in Google Workspace. You can write a letter, a notice, or a short report and work on it with other people later.

Google’s “Create, view, or download a file” page says:

  1. On your computer, open a Google Docs (or Sheets, Slides, Forms, or Vids) home screen. For a document, that home screen is docs.google.com.
  2. Click Create.

A new file is automatically named Untitled document. To rename it:

  1. Click the name at the top of the file.
  2. Type a new name.
  3. Press Enter.

When you are online, Google automatically saves your changes as you type. You do not need a Save button. If you are not connected to the internet, Google describes optional offline access — set that up only on a device you own, not on a public computer (see Google’s Drive and Docs help for those steps if you need them).

You can also download a copy: open the file, click File, then Download, and choose a file type. That is useful if someone needs a file they can open without Google Docs.

Type a short practise notice, such as “Community kitchen volunteers meet Thursday.” Use Canadian spelling. This lesson is not Microsoft Word training; if you need Word buttons, see the Range Path Word basics course.

If a file warning appears about phishing or malware, Google says to use caution. Do not ignore a warning just to finish a class task.

lessons.title: Create a Google Sheet
lessons.html:
Google Sheets is an online spreadsheet app. Google’s Sheets help says it lets you create and format spreadsheets and work with other people.

To create a spreadsheet:

  1. Open the Sheets home screen at sheets.google.com.
  2. Click New. This creates and opens your new spreadsheet.

You can also create a spreadsheet from the address sheets.google.com/create.

A new file is named Untitled spreadsheet until you rename it the same way as a Doc: click the name at the top, type a new name, and press Enter. Online changes save automatically as you type. Google’s create-and-save page notes a Sheets tip: to save, click outside of the cell you typed in.

You can add, edit, or format text, numbers, or formulas. For this lesson, keep it simple: type a header row such as Item and Amount, then a few sample numbers. This is not the Range Path Excel basics or Excel next-steps course. Those courses teach Microsoft Excel tables, charts, and functions. Here the goal is only to open Sheets, type a small list, and know the file lives in Drive.

You can also start a Sheet from Drive: click New, then choose the spreadsheet type.

Do not type real bank passwords, SINs, or another person’s private numbers into a practise sheet.

lessons.title: Share a file safely
lessons.html:
You can share a Drive file or folder and choose what other people may do. Google’s sharing page describes three roles:

  • Viewer: can view the file or folder, but cannot make changes, add comments, or share the item
  • Commenter: can make comments and suggestions
  • Editor: can open, edit, delete, or move files in a folder and add new files. Editors can also change permissions and share with others by default

To share with specific people:

  1. Go to Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, or Slides.
  2. Select the item and click Share.
  3. Enter the person’s email address.
  4. Select Viewer, Commenter, or Editor.
  5. Choose whether to notify them, then click Send or Share.

General access can be Restricted (only people you have given access) or Anyone with the link (anyone on the internet who has the link can open it without signing in). If you use a work or school account, an administrator may restrict outside sharing.

Giving “Anyone with the link” access can spread a file farther than you expect. Do not use that setting for private information. When you share a folder, files inside it inherit those permissions.

If you no longer want someone to have access, open Share, find the person, and choose Remove access.

This course is not a security audit. When you are unsure, keep the file Restricted and share only with people you know.
